name: Behnisch Architekten
bio:
Behnisch Architekten is a German architecture practice based in Stuttgart, founded in 1989 by Stefan Behnisch, son of the architect Günter Behnisch, whose own firm Behnisch & Partner designed the Munich Olympic Park and the parliament building in Bonn. It began as a city branch of his father's office and, after several changes in structure and name, took its present name in 2005. Under Stefan Behnisch it grew into an international practice, with offices in Stuttgart, Boston, Munich and Los Angeles, and a long list of schools, offices, laboratories, spas and public buildings in Europe and North America.

The Ozeaneum in Stralsund (2008), a building of the German Oceanographic Museum on the Baltic harbour, drew more than 900,000 visitors in its first year and won the European Museum of the Year Award in 2010. In Hamburg the practice built the Unilever-Haus (2009), headquarters for Unilever in Germany, Austria and Switzerland, and the Marco Polo Tower (2010). The Max Aicher Arena in Inzell (2011), a speed-skating stadium designed with Pohl Architekten, followed.

name: Berthold Lubetkin
bio:
Berthold Lubetkin (1901–1990) was a Russian-born British architect who pioneered modernist design in Britain in the 1930s. Born in Tbilisi, then in the Russian Empire, he studied in Moscow under Constructivists including Alexander Rodchenko and Vladimir Tatlin, then in Berlin, Warsaw and Paris. He moved to London in 1931 and set up the practice Tecton, working closely with the engineer Ove Arup. His conviction that "nothing is too good for ordinary people" shaped his housing and health buildings, and he received the RIBA Royal Gold Medal in 1982.

Tecton's first commission was the Gorilla House, London Zoo (1933). After the war, the Spa Green Estate in Finsbury (1949), whose foundation stone Aneurin Bevan laid, brought lifts, balconies, light from several sides and a roof terrace to working families. His last Finsbury scheme, Bevin Court (1954), has a red Constructivist staircase at its heart, under which he buried his memorial to Lenin. With Francis Skinner and Douglas Bailey he then designed estates in Bethnal Green, among them the Cranbrook Estate (1963), before giving up architecture to farm in Gloucestershire.

name: Berthold Lubetkin and Tecton
bio:
Tecton was a radical London architecture group founded in 1932 by Berthold Lubetkin with Francis Skinner, Denys Lasdun, Anthony Chitty, Lindsay Drake and others, and one of the leaders in bringing continental modernism to Britain. Its name is short for the Greek architekton, "master builder". The group worked closely with the engineer Ove Arup, whose concrete construction made its daring forms possible, and its later housing for the Borough of Finsbury became a model for Britain's post-war welfare state. Sources differ on its end: Tecton's article says it disbanded in 1939, Lubetkin's that it was dissolved in 1948.

After the Gorilla House, the group built the Penguin Pool, London Zoo (1934), whose interlocking spiral ramps cross an elliptical pool seemingly without support; it is listed Grade I. Success at London Zoo led to Dudley Zoo (1937), twelve playful modernist enclosures. Highpoint I in Highgate (1935), an apartment block, set a new standard for city living and was praised by Le Corbusier. The Finsbury Health Centre (1938), the first public commission given to a modernist group in Britain, offered free health care a decade before the National Health Service.

name: Bruno Taut
bio:
Bruno Taut (1880–1938) was a German architect, urban planner and writer, active in the Weimar years and known for his theoretical work as well as his buildings. Born in Königsberg, he founded his own firm in Berlin in 1909. His Glass Pavilion at the 1914 Werkbund Exhibition in Cologne and his utopian sketches, Alpine Architecture (1917), made him a leading Expressionist. A lifelong painter, he stood apart from other modernists in his devotion to colour. When the Nazis came to power he fled to Japan, and in 1936 moved to Turkey to teach at the Academy of Fine Arts in Istanbul, where he died.

A follower of the garden city movement, he designed Gartenstadt Falkenberg in Berlin (1916). As chief architect of the Berlin housing cooperative GEHAG from 1924, he designed large estates, among them the Hufeisensiedlung (1927), planned with the city planner Martin Wagner as a horseshoe of housing around an ice-age pond and now part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and the Wohnstadt Carl Legien (1930). In Ankara he designed the Faculty of Languages, History and Geography (1940) for Turkey's Ministry of Education.

name: Charles Girault
bio:
Charles Girault (1851–1932) was a French architect of the Beaux-Arts tradition, best known for the great exhibition buildings of the Paris Exposition of 1900. Born in Cosne-Cours-sur-Loire, he studied under Honoré Daumet at the École des Beaux-Arts in Paris and in 1880 won the Prix de Rome with a design for a children's hospital by the Mediterranean. He was elected to the Académie des Beaux-Arts in 1902 and received the RIBA Royal Gold Medal in 1920. His later career took him to Belgium, where King Leopold II commissioned several public works.

For the 1900 Exposition he won the competition for the Petit Palais (1900), a trapezoid around a garden courtyard whose columns, porch and dome echo Les Invalides across the river; it now houses the City of Paris Museum of Fine Arts. At the neighbouring Grand Palais (1900) he oversaw the work of the three other architects. In Brussels he designed the Cinquantenaire Arcade (1905) for Leopold II, and at Tervuren the Royal Museum for Central Africa (AfricaMuseum) (1910), first built as a colonial museum for the king's Congo Free State and reopened after renovation in 2018.

name: David Adjaye
bio:
David Adjaye (born 1966) is a Ghanaian-British architect who has designed buildings around the world, most famously the National Museum of African American History and Culture in Washington, D.C. Born in Dar es Salaam, Tanzania, he lived in Tanzania, Egypt, Yemen and Lebanon before moving to Britain at nine. He was knighted in 2017 and in 2021 became the first African recipient of the RIBA Royal Gold Medal. In 2023 three women who had worked in his practice accused him of sexual assault and harassment; he denied the allegations and no charges were brought.

His early work was mainly houses and studios for artists, among them the Dirty House in London (2002). The Nobel Peace Center in Oslo (2005), a showcase for the Nobel Peace Prize, followed. The Moscow School of Management Skolkovo (2010), rejects the traditional campus and gathers the school into one form to bring students together. The National Museum of African American History and Culture (2016), which he led with the Freelon Group, Davis Brody Bond and SmithGroup, rises in three inverted steps wrapped in a bronze-coloured screen inspired by a Yoruba crown.

name: E. Stewart Williams
bio:
E. Stewart Williams (1909–2005) was an American architect based in Palm Springs, California, whose mid-century modern buildings did much to shape the architecture of the Coachella Valley. The son of an architect from Dayton, Ohio, who had moved his practice to Palm Springs, he studied at Cornell and the University of Pennsylvania. In 1946 he joined his father and brother in the Palm Springs firm Williams, Williams & Williams, whose first house, in 1947, was Twin Palms for Frank Sinatra.

His houses from 1947 to the end of the 1960s, such as the Koerner House (1955), pair shed roofs and deep overhangs with large sliding glass walls, post-and-beam timber frames and built-in furniture that join inside and out. In the early 1960s he turned to the International Style, as at the Palm Springs Unified School District Educational Administrative Center (1960) and the Santa Fe Federal Savings and Loan Association (1960), a steel-framed glass pavilion inspired by Mies van der Rohe's Barcelona Pavilion, shaded by sliding perforated metal panels; it now houses the Palm Springs Art Museum's Architecture and Design Center. He later designed the Palm Springs Art Museum (1976) itself.

name: Eduardo Souto de Moura
bio:
Eduardo Souto de Moura (born 1952) is a Portuguese architect from Porto who received the Pritzker Prize in 2011 and the Wolf Prize in 2013. He studied sculpture before turning to architecture at the Porto School, where he later became a professor, and from 1974 to 1979 worked with Álvaro Siza, who encouraged him to start his own firm. He set up on his own in 1980 after winning the competition for the Casa das Artes in Porto. His early commissions were mostly modest houses in Portugal; later came shopping centres, schools, galleries and a cinema across Europe.

Between 1989 and 1997 he spent eight years turning a half-ruined 12th-century monastery in Amares into the Pousada Santa Maria do Bouro (1997). The Braga Municipal Stadium (2003), built for Euro 2004, was carved out of a hillside quarry, so that one end of the pitch faces a wall of bare rock. The Burgo Tower in Porto (2007) followed, and the Casa das Histórias Paula Rego in Cascais (2009), with its two pyramid-shaped towers in red concrete, draws on the region's historic buildings, above all the nearby Palace of Sintra.

name: Emre Arolat
bio:
Emre Arolat (born 1963) is a Turkish architect, best known for the Sancaklar Mosque. Born in Ankara, he studied architecture at Mimar Sinan University in Istanbul, graduating in 1986 and taking a master's degree in 1992 In 2004 he co-founded EAA-Emre Arolat Architecture with Gonca Paşolar. His İpekyol Textile Factory won the Aga Khan Award for Architecture in 2010, and his firm has won World Architecture Festival awards in several categories, for religious, leisure, shopping, infrastructure and cultural buildings.

The Zorlu Center in Istanbul (2013), a large mixed-use complex at the European end of the Bosphorus Bridge, was designed with Tabanlıoğlu Architects. The Sancaklar Mosque in Büyükçekmece, Istanbul (2012) is set into a slope behind rough stone walls, so that only its north side and roof can be seen; a courtyard with a teahouse and library over a shallow pool leads to a simple, cave-like prayer hall. It won its World Architecture Festival category in 2013. At The Museum Hotel Antakya (2019) the hotel floats above an archaeological site, leaving its ancient remains on view.

name: Enric Miralles
bio:
Enric Miralles (1955–2000) was a Spanish architect from Barcelona whose freely formed buildings grow out of their landscape. He graduated from the Barcelona School of Architecture in 1978, and in 1984 opened an office with his first wife, Carme Pinós, which drew international attention in the years of Spain's democratic revival. From 1993 he practised with his second wife, the Italian architect Benedetta Tagliabue, as EMBT Architects. His work drew on Alejandro de la Sota, Josep Maria Jujol, Le Corbusier, Louis Kahn, Alvar Aalto and the Russian Constructivists. He died of a brain tumour at 45.

The Igualada Cemetery (1994), designed with Pinós, cuts into the land as a river of life leading the living down to a city of the dead; Miralles is buried there. With Tagliabue he converted the Santa Caterina Market in Barcelona (2005) and designed the Gas Natural Building there (2005), whose glazed blocks cantilever out from the tower. The Scottish Parliament Building in Edinburgh (2004), his largest and most controversial project, opened years late and far over budget after his death, and went on to win the 2005 Stirling Prize.

name: Ernő Goldfinger
bio:
Ernő Goldfinger (1902–1987) was a Hungarian-born British architect and furniture designer, a key figure of modernism in Britain, best remembered for his residential tower blocks. Born in Budapest, he turned to architecture after reading Hermann Muthesius's book on the English house, moved to Paris in 1921 and studied at the École des Beaux-Arts. Perret's reinforced concrete became a lasting influence. He married Ursula Blackwell and in 1934 settled in London, where he spent the rest of his career. Ian Fleming named the James Bond villain Auric Goldfinger after him; Fleming had objected to the demolition of the Hampstead cottages that made way for his house.

Before the war he built three houses at 1–3 Willow Road in Hampstead, among them his own home, 2 Willow Road (1939), now in the care of the National Trust. Alexander Fleming House, built for the Ministry of Health and now Metro Central Heights (1963), was later listed. The 27-storey Balfron Tower in Poplar (1967) served as the model for the 31-storey Trellick Tower in Kensal Town (1972), now listed Grade II* and something of a design emblem of London.

name: Frei Otto
bio:
Frei Otto (1925–2015) was a German architect and structural engineer known for lightweight structures, above all tensile and membrane roofs such as the one over the Munich Olympic Stadium. Born in Siegmar and raised in Berlin, he studied architecture there before serving as a pilot in the Second World War; in a prisoner-of-war camp near Chartres, short of materials, he began experimenting with tents as shelter. He opened his own practice in 1952, and in 1964 founded the Institute for Lightweight Structures at the University of Stuttgart. He received the Pritzker Prize in 2015; he died the day before it was announced.

His early tent pavilions included the Tanzbrunnen (Star Wave Tent) in Cologne's Rheinpark (1957). After the West German pavilion at Expo 67 in Montreal, designed with Rolf Gutbrod, he designed the vast cable-net and acrylic roof of the Munich Olympic Stadium (1972) with Günter Behnisch. The Multihalle Mannheim (1975) followed. With Shigeru Ban and Buro Happold he worked on the Japan Pavilion, Expo 2000 in Hanover (2000), whose roof is made entirely of paper. Frei Otto's work is studied for doing the most with the least material.

name: Gerrit Rietveld
bio:
Gerrit Rietveld (1888–1964) was a Dutch furniture designer and architect and one of the leading members of the De Stijl movement. Born in Utrecht, the son of a joiner, he left school at 11 to work in his father's workshop and taught himself drawing and model-making before opening his own furniture workshop in 1917. His Red and Blue Chair, designed that year and recoloured after he joined De Stijl in 1919, became one of the best-known pieces of modern furniture. In 1928 he broke with De Stijl for a more functional architecture, joined CIAM, and experimented early with prefabricated concrete, standardisation and cheap social housing; he also designed the Zig-Zag Chair in 1934.

The Rietveld Schröder House in Utrecht (1924), designed with its owner Truus Schröder-Schräder, has an upper floor with no fixed walls, only sliding partitions that change the living space; it has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2000. The Garage with Chauffeur's Flat in Utrecht (1928) followed. After the war he rebuilt the Dutch Pavilion, Venice Biennale (1954), and he began the Van Gogh Museum in Amsterdam (1973), which was completed after his death.

name: Giuseppe Terragni
bio:
Giuseppe Terragni (1904–1943) was an Italian architect who led the Italian modern movement under the name of Rationalism, working mostly under Mussolini's fascist regime. Born in Meda in Lombardy, he studied architecture at the Polytechnic University of Milan and in 1927 opened an office in Como with his brother Attilio. In 1926 he was among the founders of Gruppo 7, whose manifesto attacked neo-classical and neo-baroque revival. His career lasted only 13 years, and most of his small body of work stands in Como, one of the centres of Italian modernism. Sent with the Italian army to the Eastern Front in the Second World War, he suffered a breakdown and died in Como in 1943.

His best-known building, the Casa del Fascio in Como (1936), the local party headquarters, is a square block 33.2 metres wide and half as high, its façade proportioned by the golden ratio, with an assembly hall lit through a glass-block skylight. With Pietro Lingeri he designed the Casa Rustici in Milan (1935), and the nursery school Asilo Sant'Elia in Como (1937) followed.

name: Grafton Architects
bio:
Grafton Architects is an Irish practice founded in Dublin in 1978 by Yvonne Farrell (born 1951) and Shelley McNamara (born 1952), who began teaching together at University College Dublin in 1976; it takes its name from the city's Grafton Street. Specialising in universities, they use weighty materials such as stone and concrete to make spacious buildings that bring people together. McNamara has described their approach: "rather than thinking of a space and then finding a structure for it, we make a structure and that, in turn, makes a space". They curated the 2018 Venice Architecture Biennale, "Freespace", and shared the Pritzker Prize in 2020, the year the practice also received the RIBA Royal Gold Medal.

The Università Luigi Bocconi Building in Milan (2008) first drew international attention to the practice. The UTEC University Campus in Lima (2015), for the University of Engineering and Technology, won the RIBA International Prize in 2016 as the best new building in the world that year. The Toulouse School of Economics (2019) followed, and the Marshall Building, London School of Economics (2022), won in competition in 2016.

name: Gunnar Asplund
bio:
Gunnar Asplund (1885–1940) was a Swedish architect, a leading figure of Nordic Classicism in the 1920s and then of the modernism that broke through in Sweden at the Stockholm Exhibition of 1930, for which he and Sigurd Lewerentz were the main architects. Its glass-and-steel entry pavilion, though temporary, was influential far beyond Sweden. From 1931 he was professor of architecture at the Royal Institute of Technology in Stockholm, marking his appointment with the lecture "Our architectonic concept of space". Alvar Aalto regarded him as a mentor, and he is often called the most important Swedish modernist architect.

The Stockholm Public Library (1928), the model work of Nordic Classicism, gathers its reading room in a tall cylindrical rotunda, partly inspired by Claude-Nicolas Ledoux, over a square base, and influenced Aalto's Viipuri Library. His long work on the Gothenburg Law Courts Extension (1937), begun in 1913, records his own change from neo-classical to functionalist architect. With Lewerentz he created the Woodland Cemetery in Stockholm (1940), shaped between 1914 and 1940 and now a UNESCO World Heritage Site; its Woodland Crematorium, finished in the year of his death, is considered his finest work.

name: Henry N. Cobb
bio:
Henry N. Cobb (1926–2020) was an American architect and a founding partner, with I. M. Pei and Eason H. Leonard, of Pei Cobb Freed & Partners in New York. Born in Boston, he studied at Harvard College and the Harvard Graduate School of Design. He chaired Harvard's Department of Architecture from 1980 to 1985 and in 2013 received the Council on Tall Buildings and Urban Habitat's Lynn S. Beedle Award.

Place Ville Marie in Montreal (1962) is a 47-storey cruciform office tower above a plaza and shopping concourse. In Boston he designed the Harbor Towers (1971), apartments built to revive the city's run-down waterfront, and the John Hancock Tower (1976), whose skin of the largest possible panes of slightly blue reflective glass, without spandrel panels and with minimal mullions, lets it fade against the sky; it has been the tallest building in New England ever since. Fountain Place in Dallas (1986) is a 60-storey tower cut as a large, many-faceted prism. Henry N. Cobb's buildings are studied for the tall building as pure geometry.

name: Henry van de Velde
bio:
Henry van de Velde (1863–1957) was a Belgian painter, architect, interior designer and theorist who, with Victor Horta and Paul Hankar, is counted among the founders of Art Nouveau in Belgium. Born in Antwerp, he trained as a painter. In 1892 he gave up painting for design, and he was among the first designers to use abstract curving lines rather than forms copied from nature. He spent the most important part of his career in Germany, where in 1907 he co-founded the German Werkbund, and in Weimar he headed the school of arts and crafts until the First World War, proposing Walter Gropius as his successor.

His first building was his own house, Villa Bloemenwerf in Uccle near Brussels (1895), inspired by William Morris's Red House and designed down to its furniture. Villa Esche in Chemnitz (1903), was his first commission in Germany. Hohenhof in Hagen (1908), the home of the patron Karl Ernst Osthaus, was conceived as a total work of art, from shell to furnishings and garden. Back in Belgium he designed the Boekentoren in Ghent (1942), the tower of the university library, which holds three million books.

name: J. J. P. Oud
bio:
J. J. P. Oud (1890–1963) was a Dutch architect who first became known as a member of the De Stijl movement. Born in Purmerend, he was influenced by H. P. Berlage, and while working with Willem Dudok in Leiden met Theo van Doesburg. From 1918 to 1933 he was municipal housing architect for Rotterdam, designing progressive workers' housing in districts such as Spangen, Kiefhoek and the Witte Dorp, and he described his aim of reconciling cheap, rational building with the needs of residents as "poetic functionalism". By 1932 he was counted with Mies van der Rohe, Gropius and Le Corbusier among the four greatest modern architects.

De Vonk in Noordwijkerhout (1918), on which he worked with Van Doesburg, belongs to his De Stijl years, and the Café De Unie in Rotterdam (1925) followed. The Kiefhoek estate in Rotterdam (1930) is one of his best-known workers' housing schemes. After the war he moved away from De Stijl and took an individual stand against mainstream modernism, designing the National Monument on Dam Square in Amsterdam and, in The Hague, the World Forum (Congress Building) (1969).

name: J. Mayer H.
bio:
J. Mayer H. is a Berlin architecture practice founded in 1996 by the German architect and artist Jürgen Mayer H. (born 1965 in Stuttgart), who studied at the University of Stuttgart, the Cooper Union and Princeton. Since 2014, when Andre Santer and Hans Schneider joined as partners, it has been called J. Mayer H. und Partner. The practice works where architecture meets communication and new technology, from urban plans and buildings to installations and objects in new materials, and its work is held in collections including the Museum of Modern Art in New York.

The Stadthaus Scharnhauser Park in Ostfildern (2002), a town hall, is in the permanent collection of the Museum of Modern Art. For Georgia it designed a series of public buildings, among them Queen Tamar Airport in Mestia (2010) and the Sarpi Border Checkpoint on the Black Sea (2011). The Metropol Parasol in Seville (2011), chosen from 65 entries in a city competition, spreads a canopy of roughly 150 by 70 metres over the Plaza de la Encarnación; known locally as Las Setas, "the mushrooms", it is marketed as the world's largest wooden structure.

name: Juan O'Gorman
bio:
Juan O'Gorman (1905–1982) was a Mexican architect and painter, a pioneer of functionalist architecture in Latin America who later turned to murals and to an architecture rooted in Mexican landscape and tradition. Born in Coyoacán, Mexico City, he graduated from the Academy of San Carlos in 1927 and studied the theories of Le Corbusier. As head of the architecture office of the Ministry of Public Education from 1932, he designed 26 primary schools in Mexico City in a spirit of "eliminating all architectural style". After six years of strict functionalism he turned to painting and murals.

In San Ángel he built the Casa O'Gorman 1929 (Cecil O'Gorman House), a small house and studio for his father that he called the first functionalist building in Latin America. Its neighbour, the Diego Rivera and Frida Kahlo House-Studio (1932), is two houses joined by a bridge. He played an essential part in building Rivera's Anahuacalli Museum (1964), made of volcanic stone quarried on its own site. His best-known work, the Central Library (UNAM) (1956), is wrapped in some 4,000 square metres of mosaic murals of coloured stones he gathered across Mexico.

name: Kashef Mahboob Chowdhury
bio:
Kashef Mahboob Chowdhury (born 1970) is a Bangladeshi architect based in Dhaka whose work is rooted in history, climate, materials and place. Born in Dhaka, the son of a civil engineer, he grew up in Bangladesh and the Middle East, graduated in architecture from the Bangladesh University of Engineering and Technology in 1995, and in 2006 attended Glenn Murcutt's masterclass in Sydney. In 1995 he founded the practice URBANA with Marina Tabassum and has led it as principal since 2005. His studio gives projects long periods of research and for years worked only by daylight, a sign of the respect for time that critics have noted in his work.

With Tabassum he won the 1997 competition for the Swadhinata Stambha in Dhaka (2013), whose 50-metre tower of stacked glass panels stands where the Pakistani surrender was signed in 1971. The Friendship Centre in Gaibandha (2011) won the Aga Khan Award for Architecture in the 2014–16 cycle. The Gulshan Society Mosque in Dhaka (2017) is a seven-storey white concrete monolith wrapped in a screen that forms the words "La-ilaha-illallah" in Kufic script.

name: Kazuo Shinohara
bio:
Kazuo Shinohara (1925–2006) was a Japanese architect, theorist and teacher whose influence runs through much of contemporary Japanese architecture. He studied at the Tokyo Institute of Technology, finishing in 1953, opened his own practice in 1954, and became a professor there in 1970. The critic Thomas Daniell called him "a key figure who explicitly rejected Western influences yet appears on almost every branch of the family tree of contemporary Japanese architecture". The so-called Shinohara School is linked to Toyo Ito, Kazunari Sakamoto, Itsuko Hasegawa, Kazuyo Sejima and Ryue Nishizawa. He received the Architectural Institute of Japan's grand prize in 2005, and in 2010 the Venice Biennale awarded a special Golden Lion in his memory.

Most of his work was houses, more than 30 of them, generally described as lucid and ephemeral. The Umbrella House (Kasa no Ie) (1961) was one of the first, and the House in White (1966) belongs to the same series of early houses in Tokyo. From the 1980s he turned to larger public buildings, among them the Japan Ukiyo-e Museum in Matsumoto (1982) and the Centennial Hall, Tokyo Institute of Technology (1987).

name: Kevin Roche
bio:
Kevin Roche (1922–2019) was an Irish-born American architect who received the Pritzker Prize in 1982. Born in Dublin, he graduated from University College Dublin and went to the United States to study under Mies van der Rohe at the Illinois Institute of Technology. He became principal designer for Eero Saarinen and after Saarinen's death formed his own firm with the engineer John Dinkeloo in 1966. Together they designed more than 200 built projects, and from 1967 he drew up the master plan for the Metropolitan Museum of Art and designed all its new wings.

The firm's first major commission, the Oakland Museum of California (1969), is a set of terraces and roof gardens for art, natural history and cultural history. The Ford Foundation Building in New York (1967) wraps its offices around a large garden atrium, the first such space in a Manhattan office building, behind a cube of glass and steel. The Cummins Corporate Office Building in Columbus, Indiana (1983) is built around the company's first factory. Late in life he returned to Ireland for the Convention Centre Dublin (2010), with its glass front and curving walls.

name: Kevin Roche John Dinkeloo and Associates
bio:
Kevin Roche John Dinkeloo and Associates (KRJDA), also known as Roche-Dinkeloo, was an American architecture firm based in Hamden, Connecticut. It was created in 1966 out of Eero Saarinen & Associates, which Saarinen, who died in 1961, had asked to be renamed within five years of his death. Kevin Roche led the design and John Dinkeloo, was the expert in construction and technology. The firm completed more than 200 projects in the United States and abroad, and its style moved from massive façades of exposed steel and concrete to clean glass buildings. It won the AIA Architecture Firm Award in 1974, and in 2020 it moved to New Haven as Roche Modern.

The Knights of Columbus Building in New Haven (1969) sets a tower between four cylindrical corner towers, standing for the four principles of the Catholic order; locals call it the "Tootsie Roll Building". The Power Center for the Performing Arts at the University of Michigan (1971) and The Pyramids (College Life Insurance) in Indianapolis (1972) followed. name: Lacaton & Vassal
bio:
Lacaton & Vassal is a French architecture practice founded in Bordeaux in 1987 by Anne Lacaton (born 1955) and Jean-Philippe Vassal (born 1954); the practice moved to Paris in 2000. In Niger, where Vassal worked in the early 1980s, they formed their guiding idea: "never demolish what could be redeemed". They are known for transforming existing social housing rather than tearing it down, and for doing more with cheap materials and greenhouse construction, which gives homes extra winter-garden space at low cost. They received the Pritzker Prize in 2021 for what the jury called a "restorative architecture".

The House in Cap Ferret (1998) was one of their early private houses. At the Nantes School of Architecture (2009), 5,500 square metres of floor are left without a fixed use, to be taken over as the school needs. For FRAC Nord-Pas de Calais in Dunkirk (2013) they kept a large harbour boathouse intact and built a twin beside it to house the contemporary art collection. In the Grand Parc Bordeaux Transformation (2016), they cut away the old façade panels of occupied housing blocks to add balconies and large sliding windows.

name: Lina Bo Bardi
bio:
Lina Bo Bardi (1914–1992) was an Italian-born Brazilian modernist architect and designer who devoted her working life to the social and cultural potential of architecture. Born in Rome, she graduated in architecture there in 1939, worked in Milan with Carlo Pagani and Gio Ponti. In 1946 she married the critic Pietro Maria Bardi and moved with him to Brazil, where they founded the magazine Habitat and he set up the São Paulo Museum of Art. Drawn to Brazilian vernacular design, she found acceptance hard as both a foreigner and a woman. In 2021 the Venice Biennale gave her a posthumous Special Golden Lion for Lifetime Achievement.

Her first built work was her own Casa de Vidro (1951), a glass house in the remnants of the Atlantic rainforest in Morumbi, São Paulo. In Salvador she turned a 17th-century sugar mill into the museum of the Solar do Unhão (1963). MASP (1968), the São Paulo Museum of Art, lifts its galleries in a box spanning 74 metres on four red concrete columns. SESC Pompéia (1986) converts a factory into a leisure centre, with two concrete sports towers joined by walkways.

name: MAD Architects
bio:
MAD Architects is a Chinese design practice founded in 2004 by Ma Yansong, who leads it with the partners Dang Qun and Yosuke Hayano. From its base in China it has built museums, theatres, housing, hotels and offices in China and abroad. Since 2013 it has set out its ideas for the city in "Shanshui City" exhibitions in Beijing, Berlin and at the 2014 Venice Architecture Biennale.

The Ordos Museum in Inner Mongolia (2011), a large open-plan space with six levels of galleries, was influenced by the Gobi Desert and the work of Buckminster Fuller. The Sheraton Huzhou Hot Spring Resort (2013) was followed by the Harbin Opera House (2015), clad entirely in white aluminium panels at the heart of a cultural island in the wetlands of the Songhua River. Quzhou Stadium (2022) sets its stands into a landscaped park under a 250-metre floating membrane roof and has been described as a work of "land art". MAD's buildings are studied for curving forms drawn from nature.

name: Mansilla + Tuñón
bio:
Mansilla + Tuñón was a Spanish architecture practice founded in Madrid in 1992 by Luis Moreno Mansilla (1959–2012) and Emilio Tuñón (born 1958), both from Madrid; it worked until Mansilla's death in 2012. The two taught at the Madrid school of architecture, ETSAM, and at Harvard, the EPFL in Lausanne, the Städelschule in Frankfurt and Princeton, and in 2009 they directed the Spanish Architecture Biennial. Much of their work came from public competitions for museums, libraries and cultural centres across Spain, and in 2014 the practice received Spain's Gold Medal of Merit in the Fine Arts.

The Museu de Belles Arts de Castelló (2001), won in a 1997 competition, was followed in León by the Auditorio Ciudad de León (2002). Their best-known building, MUSAC, Museum of Contemporary Art of Castilla y León (2004), won the 2007 Mies van der Rohe Award, the European Union Prize for Contemporary Architecture. In Madrid they won the competition for the Royal Collections Gallery (2023) in 2002; set beside the Royal Palace and Almudena Cathedral, it holds the collections of the Spanish crown. They also won the 2007 competition for Madrid's International Convention Center.

name: Nayyar Ali Dada
bio:
Nayyar Ali Dada (born 1943) is a Pakistani architect based in Lahore, known above all for the Alhamra Arts Council in Lahore. Born in Delhi, he moved with his family to Lahore in the 1950s, graduated from the National College of Arts in 1964 and stayed on to teach there. His friendship with the college's principal, the painter Shakir Ali, led to his design for Ali's house in Garden Town, now the Shakir Ali Museum. Buildings associated with him and his practice, Nayyar Ali Dada & Associates, include museums, mosques, hotels, a cancer hospital, a university campus and the restoration of Lahore's historic Bagh-e-Jinnah garden.

His best-known work, the Alhamra Arts Council in Lahore (1992), began as a 1,000-seat auditorium and grew with a hexagonal theatre and an octagonal lecture hall, built of handmade red brick over concrete in the manner of the Lahore Fort and Badshahi Mosque; it won the Aga Khan Award for Architecture in 1998. The Lahore Expo Centre (2010) was designed with NESPAK, and the Grand Jamia Mosque, Bahria Town (2014) is a large later work.
